prime.problem: The tokenizer gives the model integers, but every layer after it multiplies and adds vectors. Feed it the raw ID and the model treats sat = 2 as "twice cat", an order and a size that the word list never meant.
prime.fits: First step of the forward pass. It reuses the matmul from the tools cards: a lookup is a one-hot row times a matrix. The next card adds position information to the same rows.
expect: a gradient only for rows that were read
prime.goal: Compute \(x_0\) for the cat sat from \(E\) and \(P\) by hand, show the lookup equals \(\operatorname{onehot}(\mathit{id})\, E\), and say which rows of \(E\) a backward pass can change.

attend: Which row of \(E\) does each 0 in a one-hot vector wipe out, and what does that same 0 do to the gradient on the way back?
If a token's vector were its ID times one vector, what would be forced about the, cat, sat and on?
Why does the model compute a lookup when the maths is written as a matrix product?
What does the \(P\) table add that \(E[\ids]\) can't, and what is the size of \(P\) tied to?
A token appears twice in the input: what happens to its row of \(dE\)?

must: IDs are labels in list order → feeding the ID as a number makes each vector a multiple of one direction → the = 0 is all zeros and sat is forced halfway between cat and on (rank 1) → a table gives each token an independent row (\(E\) has rank 4)

\(\operatorname{onehot}(\mathit{id})\, E\) scales every row by 0 except row \(\mathit{id}\) → the product equals \(E[\mathit{id}]\) exactly (difference 0.0) → so the lookup is an ordinary linear layer that backprop can train → but 16 of 20 multiply-adds are by zero, so real code copies the row instead
Going forward, the 0s in the one-hot block rows 3 and 4 (on, mat) → those rows never affect the loss → their gradient is exactly 0 → one SGD step moves only the rows that were read
Same token in two slots → its row is read twice → \(dE\) for that row is the sum of the two slots' gradients (the the cat cat run: row 1 = slot 1 + slot 2)
elevated: Tied embeddings (Qwen, original GPT-2): \(E\) is also the output head → every row gets a gradient from the output scores on every step → the "unread rows get 0" rule only holds with a separate output head, as in the tiny model and Raschka's GPT

compress.prompt: From memory, in 3–4 sentences: how does an ID become \(x_0\), why is that lookup the same as a one-hot product, and why isn't the ID used directly? Or draw \(\operatorname{onehot}(0)\, E\) for the, with the rows that get wiped out.
checklist: each ID picks one row of a learned table \(E\); positions add a row of \(P\)
\(\operatorname{onehot}(\mathit{id})\, E\) zeroes every row but one, so it equals the lookup exactly
the ID as a number would impose order and size: all tokens on one line, ID 0 always zero
the entries of \(E\) are weights that training moves
only rows that were read get a gradient (with a separate output head)

retrieve.q: Explain why an embedding table is a weight matrix and not just a data structure.
answer: the lookup equals \(\operatorname{onehot}(\mathit{id})\, E\), a linear layer
so the loss has a gradient with respect to each entry of \(E\)
training updates those entries like any other weight

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens to the cat sat \(= [0,\ 1,\ 2]\) from IDs to \(x_0\), with shapes.
answer: 3 IDs pick rows 0, 1, 2 of \(E\) (\(5 \times 4\)), giving \(E[\ids]\) of \(3 \times 4\)

retrieve.q: Qwen has a 151,936-token vocabulary with \(d_{\text{model}} = 896\). Compare computing one token's embedding as \(\operatorname{onehot}(\mathit{id})\, E\) with a lookup. What does each cost, and what do you lose by using the lookup?
answer: one-hot product: 136,134,656 multiply-adds per token, almost all by zero
you lose nothing: the result and the gradient are the same; the one-hot form stays useful as a way to reason about it

compare.q: This card adds a learned \(P\) row to each token. The next card rotates \(Q\) and \(K\) instead. What does each one change, and why does a learned \(P\) table stop working past its length?
answer: learned \(P\): a learned vector added to \(x_0\), one per slot
RoPE: no table; queries and keys are rotated by an angle that grows with position
\(P\) has one row per slot, so a longer input has no row to look up
RoPE's score depends only on the distance between positions

compare.q: A one-hot row times \(E\) and a dense row times \(W\) are the same operation. What makes the one-hot case special, both for the cost and for the gradient?
answer: one-hot has one nonzero entry, so the product is a single row of \(E\)
the cost drops from \(\text{vocab} \times d_{\text{model}}\) multiply-adds to a copy
the gradient for \(W\) from a dense input reaches every row; from a one-hot input it reaches only row \(\mathit{id}\)

predict.q: Feed the tiny model the the the (IDs \([0,\ 0,\ 0]\)). How many rows of \(dE\) are nonzero, how is row 0 built, and does \(x_0\) have three identical rows?
predict.answer: One row: row 0, which is the sum of the gradients from all three slots. The rows of \(x_0\) are not identical, because each slot adds a different row of \(P\): that's the only thing telling the three copies of the apart.

apply.task: Change inputs in llm-math/labs/tiny.py to np.array([0, 1, 1]) (the cat cat) and run it. Check that \(dE[1] = dP[1] + dP[2]\), entry by entry.
apply.hint: In this model \(dP\) equals \(dx_0\), the gradient arriving at \(x_0\), one row per slot.
